newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo 1996 steel production seen at 650,000 tonnes.
newsitem.headline: Yugo 1996 steel production seen at 650,000 tonnes.

text.p: Yugoslavia's 1996 steel output should reach 650,000 tonnes by the end of the year and return to its pre-sanctions level, the head of the Yugoslav Association of Ferrous Metallurgy said on Monday.
"If we manage to maintain the current dynamics of producing about 65,000 tonnes of steel a month, our total 1996 output will hit 650,000 tonnes, last seen in 1992," Arsenije Jovanovic told Reuters.
Steel production jumped by 68,684 tonnes in August, bringing the January-August figure to 362,195 tonnes, the association said in its monthly report.
According to the report, the largest Yugoslav steelworks of Smederevo produced 57,900 tonnes of steel in August, below 64,165 tonnes produced a month earlier.
Another 10,784 tonnes were produced by the Niksic steel factory, the report said.
Jovanovic said this year's results were impressive since they were achieved in the year following a partial suspension of the 3-1/2 years of international trade embargo.
"Most of the help came from our traditional trading partners who provided financial help needed to revive production.
However, Yugoslav steelmakers still faced bitter and unfair competition from Eastern European suppliers, who deliever their goods at dumping prices.

"Almost 14 percent of the total Yugoslav ferrous metallurgy imports enters the country at prices lower than those at the western markets, and most of the unfair competition comes from the neighbouring Bulgaria and Romania," Jovanovic said.
Those were followed by Ukraine and Russian suppliers.

Yugoslav steelmakers deny they are trying to protect their monopolist position and claim that import quotas are too massive for the market, shrunken after the violent breakup of the former Yugoslav federation.

"We are not calling for a closed market or protective measures. We simply want domestic ferrous metallurgy to find its place in this small and limited market, now forcing us to export around half of what we produce," he said.

Jovanovic said members of the association on Tuesday will meet government representatives to discuss progress made since their last July meeting that ended with renewed calls for more orderly observing of regulations.

"There has been some improvement, but we need to see what more can be done to help the industry regain its pre-sanctions strength," Jovanovic said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
